In the following appendix , we derive the entropy of adsorption in the case of infinite dilution and show how it may be related to familiar thermodynamic quantities ( cf . eq 5 ) . To begin , we define our adsorption entropy in the limit of infinite dilution via $$ \Delta s_{\mathrm{ads}}^{\infty}=\lim_{N/V\rightarrow0}\left[\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial N}\right)_{V,T,\mathrm{ads}}-\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial N}\right)_{V,T,\mathrm{gas}}\right] $$ $$ =S_{ads}(N=1,V,T)-S_{gas}(N=1,V,T) $$ where the subscripts “ads” and “gas” labels identify the adsorbed (confined) and gas (bulk) phases, respectively. Given the constraints of a fixed number of molecules (N), volume (V), and temperature (T), it is natural to continue working in the canonical ensemble. (As in the main text, lowercase symbols identify intensive molecular or molar properties, whereas the uppercase indicates an extensive property.) For the molecules that we examine in this work (e.g., rigid molecules with no internal degrees of freedom), the canonical partition function Q may be expressed as $$ \begin{aligned}Q(N,V,T)&=Q_{trans}(N,V,T)Q_{rot}(N,V,T)\\&\quad\times Z(N,V,T)\end{aligned} $$ where $ Q_{trans} $ and $ Q_{rot} $ are the translational and rotational partition functions (which are unaffected by confinement) and Z is the configurational partition function. However, performing experiments for many molecule-framework combinations is impractical. Computational experiments of adsorption therefore make for an attractive alternative. Nevertheless, there remain caveats. For example, quantifying the entropy using ab initio-based methods (such as density functional theory) is computationally demanding $ ^{18-22} $ or relies on approximations. $ ^{19} $ Such approximations include (1) limiting translation to the surface area of the zeolite, $ ^{23} $ which artificially restricts the entropy to a surface term; (2) invocation of the “harmonic approximation” based on the assumption of a very strong fluid–solid interaction that renders translations and rotations unimportant; or (3) employing the hindered translator/rotor model. $ ^{24} $ On the other hand, (classical) Monte Carlo (MC) and molecular dynamics simulations have proven successful in accurately calculating the adsorption entropy, $ ^{25} $ with the primary limitation being the number of force fields available to accurately model the adsorbate–adsorbent interaction. Although these simulations are numerically cleaner compared to experiment because they involve analyzing efficiently a greater number of molecule–zeolite combinations, it remains overwhelming to apply them to the millions of hypothetical frameworks. Novel topology-based, data-driven approaches have been shown to be adequate in predicting specific features such as adsorption capacity $ ^{6} $ and selectivity. $ ^{26} $ However, there are currently no similar models for entropy.

final_candidate.name: size_bottleneck_confinement_ratio
final_candidate.hypothesis: At fixed framework bottleneck (lsd_f), a larger adsorbate (larger Vol, hence larger Vol^(1/3)) is more geometrically confined at the framework bottleneck, so a larger fraction of its gas-phase translational/rotational entropy is lost on adsorption, increasing loss = (Sgas - Sads)/R. Equivalently, at fixed adsorbate volume, frameworks with a larger passing free-sphere bottleneck (lsd_f) impose weaker confinement and smaller entropy loss. This is a conditional geometric-confinement hypothesis motivated by reported FER/FAU and MFI/FAU comparisons (E02, E04), not an established law for this dataset.
final_candidate.rationale: Vol^(1/3) converts the van der Waals volume into an isotropic linear size proxy; lsd_f (Zeo++ Df) is the largest sphere that can pass through a periodic free path, i.e., the tightest geometric constraint on guest passage, not the global cavity diameter Di. The ratio proxies the tightness of geometric confinement without claiming a literal free-volume equality: both factors are length-like, the ratio is dimensionless, and both native inputs are strictly positive over the entire training support (Vol in [20.424, 161.144] angstrom^3; lsd_f in [0.85684, 7.68726] angstrom), so no native-zero handling is required. Known limitations: (i) Df is a bottleneck, so a molecule can sit in a large cage behind a narrow window and this descriptor then overestimates local confinement; (ii) Vol^(1/3) ignores molecular anisotropy, which PBF/PMI/SPAN would capture but only with rotor_case branching and legitimate zeros; (iii) AV is deliberately not used because it is mass-specific fixed-probe accessibility, not molecule-specific free volume.

draft.name: size_bottleneck_confinement_ratio
draft.hypothesis: At fixed framework bottleneck (lsd_f), a larger adsorbate (larger Vol, hence larger Vol^(1/3)) is more geometrically confined at the framework bottleneck, so a larger fraction of its gas-phase translational/rotational entropy is lost on adsorption, increasing loss = (Sgas - Sads)/R. Equivalently, at fixed adsorbate volume, frameworks with a larger passing free-sphere bottleneck (lsd_f) impose weaker confinement and smaller entropy loss. This is a conditional geometric-confinement hypothesis motivated by reported FER/FAU and MFI/FAU comparisons (E02, E04), not an established law for this dataset.
draft.rationale: Vol^(1/3) converts the van der Waals volume into an isotropic linear size proxy; lsd_f (Zeo++ Df) is the largest sphere that can pass through a periodic free path, i.e., the tightest geometric constraint on guest passage, not the global cavity diameter Di. The ratio proxies the tightness of geometric confinement without claiming a literal free-volume equality: both factors are length-like, the ratio is dimensionless, and both native inputs are strictly positive over the entire training support (Vol in [20.424, 161.144] angstrom^3; lsd_f in [0.85684, 7.68726] angstrom), so no native-zero handling is required. Known limitations: (i) Df is a bottleneck, so a molecule can sit in a large cage behind a narrow window and this descriptor then overestimates local confinement; (ii) Vol^(1/3) ignores molecular anisotropy, which PBF/PMI/SPAN would capture but only with rotor_case branching and legitimate zeros; (iii) AV is deliberately not used because it is mass-specific fixed-probe accessibility, not molecule-specific free volume.
draft.falsification_criteria: The hypothesis is falsified if, holding Vol fixed, the learned loss decreases with this descriptor (opposite sign to confinement), or if the association vanishes once probe-accessible area/volume (q_ASA, q_AV) are controlled for, indicating the descriptor only re-expresses accessibility rather than bottleneck confinement. A competing explanation to rule out: descriptor behavior driven entirely by lsd_f correlating with framework density rather than any adsorbate-size dependence (check by testing whether the Vol dependence holds at fixed lsd_f).
draft.proxy_assumptions: Assumes (1) geometric confinement at the tightest passage is a relevant driver of adsorption entropy loss, by analogy to reported cavity-diameter/rotational-entropy-loss comparisons, which used cavity diameters, not Df — this proxy mapping is assumed, not demonstrated; (2) Vol^(1/3) is an adequate isotropic molecular size proxy; (3) q-normalization with fixed positive training references preserves monotonic ordering (q_Vol and q_lsd_f are strictly positive scalings). No causal claim: the descriptor is an empirical proxy and the direction of the target association is a hypothesis to be tested.
draft.boundary_behavior: Finite training support: q_Vol in [(20.424/67.24), (161.144/67.24)] and q_lsd_f in [(0.85684/5.16326), (7.68726/5.16326)], both strictly positive, so the ratio is finite and strictly positive everywhere in the training domain. review_issues.explanation: The cited mechanism comparisons (E02: FER vs FAU rotational entropy loss vs average cavity diameter; E04: MFI vs FAU for linear alkanes) use average cavity diameter Di as the confinement descriptor, while the draft uses lsd_f (Zeo++ Df, the largest passing free sphere along a periodic path). Df is a bottleneck/window quantity, not a cavity diameter; the source-to-descriptor proxy mapping (Df standing in for Di) is assumed, not demonstrated. The draft acknowledges this, but the evidentiary support remains indirect.

E06 concerns MCM-22 supercages, where rotational freedom differences were only qualitatively analyzed by comparing radius of gyration to space available inside the cage; it does not address bottleneck/window passage, which is what lsd_f measures. Using E06 to motivate a bottleneck-based size ratio extends the source claim beyond its scope (cage occupancy vs window passage). Source conditions also flag diffusion discussion at 450–850 K and MCM-22-specific behavior.

The source percentages (e.g., 38% vs 20% entropy loss) and the 3-fold rotational-loss comparison are specific to the reported framework/adsorbate pairs and conditions (temperature, loading, framework chemistry unresolved in the excerpts). The draft does not import these numbers, but its directional hypothesis (smaller confinement dimension -> larger entropy loss) transferred to pure-silica rigid frameworks at infinite dilution remains an untested transfer assumption per C1/C2/C4.

Vol**(1/3) is an isotropic linear size proxy; the actual confinement-relevant dimension is the molecule's cross-section along the bottleneck path, which depends on orientation and shape (anistropy captured only by PBF/PMI/SPAN/GeDi, which are heavy-atom/implicit-H proxies with legitimate zeros and would require rotor_case branching). The draft states this limitation, but it means the descriptor can mis-rank elongated vs compact adsorbates of equal volume.

Df as a bottleneck can overestimate local confinement for molecules residing in large cages behind narrow windows (draft acknowledges). E06 indicates adsorption in MCM-22 occurs predominantly in supercages, i.e., situations where bottleneck Df and cage interior dimensions diverge; the descriptor's relevance in cage-dominated frameworks is therefore uncertain rather than established.

The claimed direction (entropy loss decreasing in lsd_f at fixed Vol; loss increasing in the descriptor) is a hypothesis with no target values provided in this input; no label-based check of the association exists. The derivative/limit checks passed are purely structural (monotonicity of the formula, structural_checks_passed_semantics_unverified) and do not verify the physical prediction or the mechanism.

The hypothesis mixes translational and rotational entropy loss ('a larger fraction of its gas-phase translational/rotational entropy is lost'), but the cited comparisons E02/E04 specifically concern rotational entropy loss; the translational-rotational contribution statement (E03) is not among the draft's cited evidence ids. The translational component of the claimed mechanism is thus only weakly supported by the cited set.

The structured limit (descriptor -> 0 as lsd_f -> +infinity) is a formal extrapolation outside the training support (lsd_f max 7.68726 angstrom); no empirical data constrain behavior near the limit. Additionally, q-normalization means the descriptor equals a constant times Vol**(1/3)/lsd_f; the constant rescaling does not affect ordering, but any interpretation of a threshold (descriptor = 1 as an equality of size and bottleneck) would be a normalization artifact, not a native physical equality.

Knowledge-graph edges from the conditional mechanisms to lsd_f/Vol are MAY_USE_PROXY_UNDER_ASSUMPTIONS entries, and absence of further graph support is unknown, not disproof; transfer of the reported MFI/FAU and FER/FAU behavior to the benchmark's framework population, and any confounding of lsd_f with framework density (flagged in the draft's own falsification criteria), remain unverified.

final_candidate.name: pmi_anisotropy_reg
final_candidate.hypothesis: Conditional hypothesis (rotation/shape family): at fixed framework geometry (e.g., fixed lsd_f, lsd_p, AV), adsorbates with larger principal-moment anisotropy (PMI3 - PMI1)/(PMI3 + PMI1) lose a larger fraction of their gas-phase rotational entropy upon adsorption, because anisotropic (elongated or disk-like) guests have orientation-dependent accessibility: rotations about the short axes sweep a volume comparable to the molecular length/width scale and are more strongly hindered in pores than the nearly isotropic rotations of compact guests. This generalizes the reported MFI-vs-FAU rotational-loss comparison (E01, E04) and the FER/FAU cavity-confinement comparison (E02), and follows the MCM-22 proposal to compare molecular rotational freedom via a molecular size/shape measure (radius of gyration) against the available cavity space (E06), consistent with rotation being a distinct contributor to entropy loss alongside translation (E03). This is an empirical, unverified mechanism for this dataset, not an established law; the competing expectation that a rod aligned in a straight channel rotates freely about its long axis is explicitly acknowledged as a falsification route.
final_candidate.rationale: PMI3 and PMI1 are heavy-atom, implicit-H inertia proxies, not full all-atom moments; the +1.0 (in the native amu*angstrom^2 scale) is a fixed regularization constant that keeps the descriptor finite at legitimate physical zeros (single-site atoms with all PMIs = 0 map to 0, i.e., rotationally spherical, which is physically appropriate since a monatomic guest has no rotational entropy to lose). Because it is a dimensionless ratio of native quantities, no q-normalization is needed and no q-ratio is misread as a physical equality threshold. The descriptor is a shape proxy only; it does not encode pore size, so any claimed effect is conditional on holding the framework inputs fixed. It does not duplicate the round-2 size-vs-bottleneck descriptor (q_Vol**(1/3)/q_lsd_f) and targets a different mechanism family (rotation rather than translational size confinement).
final_candidate.falsification_criteria: Falsified if, holding the used framework inputs (lsd_f, lsd_p, AV) fixed, adsorption entropy loss does not increase with the anisotropy descriptor over its training range, or if the apparent anisotropy effect disappears once Vol (overall size) is controlled for, indicating size rather than shape drives the loss. Also falsified if elongated guests in straight-channel frameworks retain rotational entropy (free rotation about the long axis after alignment), giving the opposite sign in that regime. Boundary check: single-site guests (PMI1 = PMI3 = 0) must show the minimum descriptor value 0; if these guests show nonzero relative rotational loss attributable to shape, the proxy mapping fails.

To begin , we define our adsorption entropy in the limit of infinite dilution via $$ \Delta s_{\mathrm{ads}}^{\infty}=\lim_{N/V\rightarrow0}\left[\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial N}\right)_{V,T,\mathrm{ads}}-\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial N}\right)_{V,T,\mathrm{gas}}\right] $$ $$ =S_{ads}(N=1,V,T)-S_{gas}(N=1,V,T) $$ where the subscripts “ads” and “gas” labels identify the adsorbed (confined) and gas (bulk) phases, respectively. Given the constraints of a fixed number of molecules (N), volume (V), and temperature (T), it is natural to continue working in the canonical ensemble. (As in the main text, lowercase symbols identify intensive molecular or molar properties, whereas the uppercase indicates an extensive property.) For the molecules that we examine in this work (e.g., rigid molecules with no internal degrees of freedom), the canonical partition function Q may be expressed as $$ \begin{aligned}Q(N,V,T)&=Q_{trans}(N,V,T)Q_{rot}(N,V,T)\\&\quad\times Z(N,V,T)\end{aligned} $$ where $ Q_{trans} $ and $ Q_{rot} $ are the translational and rotational partition functions (which are unaffected by confinement) and Z is the configurational partition function. The translational and rotational partition functions are available in the usual statistical mechanics texts $ ^{44,45} $ but are ultimately unimportant for the derivation that follows. However, performing experiments for many molecule-framework combinations is impractical. Computational experiments of adsorption therefore make for an attractive alternative. Nevertheless, there remain caveats. For example, quantifying the entropy using ab initio-based methods (such as density functional theory) is computationally demanding $ ^{18-22} $ or relies on approximations. $ ^{19} $ Such approximations include (1) limiting translation to the surface area of the zeolite, $ ^{23} $ which artificially restricts the entropy to a surface term; (2) invocation of the “harmonic approximation” based on the assumption of a very strong fluid–solid interaction that renders translations and rotations unimportant; or (3) employing the hindered translator/rotor model. $ ^{24} $ On the other hand, (classical) Monte Carlo (MC) and molecular dynamics simulations have proven successful in accurately calculating the adsorption entropy, $ ^{25} $ with the primary limitation being the number of force fields available to accurately model the adsorbate–adsorbent interaction. Although these simulations are numerically cleaner compared to experiment because they involve analyzing efficiently a greater number of molecule–zeolite combinations, it remains overwhelming to apply them to the millions of hypothetical frameworks. Novel topology-based, data-driven approaches have been shown to be adequate in predicting specific features such as adsorption capacity $ ^{6} $ and selectivity. $ ^{26} $ However, there are currently no similar models for entropy.

descriptor_candidate.hypothesis: Conditional hypothesis (rotation/shape family): at fixed framework geometry (e.g., fixed lsd_f, lsd_p, AV), adsorbates with larger principal-moment anisotropy (PMI3 - PMI1)/(PMI3 + PMI1) lose a larger fraction of their gas-phase rotational entropy upon adsorption, because anisotropic (elongated or disk-like) guests have orientation-dependent accessibility: rotations about the short axes sweep a volume comparable to the molecular length/width scale and are more strongly hindered in pores than the nearly isotropic rotations of compact guests. This generalizes the reported MFI-vs-FAU rotational-loss comparison (E01, E04) and the FER/FAU cavity-confinement comparison (E02), and follows the MCM-22 proposal to compare molecular rotational freedom via a molecular size/shape measure (radius of gyration) against the available cavity space (E06), consistent with rotation being a distinct contributor to entropy loss alongside translation (E03). This is an empirical, unverified mechanism for this dataset, not an established law; the competing expectation that a rod aligned in a straight channel rotates freely about its long axis is explicitly acknowledged as a falsification route.
descriptor_candidate.rationale: PMI3 and PMI1 are heavy-atom, implicit-H inertia proxies, not full all-atom moments; the +1.0 (in the native amu*angstrom^2 scale) is a fixed regularization constant that keeps the descriptor finite at legitimate physical zeros (single-site atoms with all PMIs = 0 map to 0, i.e., rotationally spherical, which is physically appropriate since a monatomic guest has no rotational entropy to lose). Because it is a dimensionless ratio of native quantities, no q-normalization is needed and no q-ratio is misread as a physical equality threshold. The descriptor is a shape proxy only; it does not encode pore size, so any claimed effect is conditional on holding the framework inputs fixed. It does not duplicate the round-2 size-vs-bottleneck descriptor (q_Vol**(1/3)/q_lsd_f) and targets a different mechanism family (rotation rather than translational size confinement).
descriptor_candidate.falsification_criteria: Falsified if, holding the used framework inputs (lsd_f, lsd_p, AV) fixed, adsorption entropy loss does not increase with the anisotropy descriptor over its training range, or if the apparent anisotropy effect disappears once Vol (overall size) is controlled for, indicating size rather than shape drives the loss. Also falsified if elongated guests in straight-channel frameworks retain rotational entropy (free rotation about the long axis after alignment), giving the opposite sign in that regime. Boundary check: single-site guests (PMI1 = PMI3 = 0) must show the minimum descriptor value 0; if these guests show nonzero relative rotational loss attributable to shape, the proxy mapping fails.

draft.name: pmi_anisotropy_reg
draft.hypothesis: Conditional hypothesis (rotation/shape family): at fixed framework geometry (e.g., fixed lsd_f, lsd_p, AV), adsorbates with larger principal-moment anisotropy (PMI3 - PMI1)/(PMI3 + PMI1) lose a larger fraction of their gas-phase rotational entropy upon adsorption, because anisotropic (elongated or disk-like) guests have orientation-dependent accessibility: rotations about the short axes sweep a volume comparable to the molecular length/width scale and are more strongly hindered in pores than the nearly isotropic rotations of compact guests. This generalizes the reported MFI-vs-FAU rotational-loss comparison (E01, E04) and the FER/FAU cavity-confinement comparison (E02), and follows the MCM-22 proposal to compare molecular rotational freedom via a molecular size/shape measure (radius of gyration) against the available cavity space (E06), consistent with rotation being a distinct contributor to entropy loss alongside translation (E03). This is an empirical, unverified mechanism for this dataset, not an established law; the competing expectation that a rod aligned in a straight channel rotates freely about its long axis is explicitly acknowledged as a falsification route.
draft.rationale: PMI3 and PMI1 are heavy-atom, implicit-H inertia proxies, not full all-atom moments; the +1.0 (in the native amu*angstrom^2 scale) is a fixed regularization constant that keeps the descriptor finite at legitimate physical zeros (single-site atoms with all PMIs = 0 map to 0, i.e., rotationally spherical, which is physically appropriate since a monatomic guest has no rotational entropy to lose). Because it is a dimensionless ratio of native quantities, no q-normalization is needed and no q-ratio is misread as a physical equality threshold. The descriptor is a shape proxy only; it does not encode pore size, so any claimed effect is conditional on holding the framework inputs fixed. It does not duplicate the round-2 size-vs-bottleneck descriptor (q_Vol**(1/3)/q_lsd_f) and targets a different mechanism family (rotation rather than translational size confinement).
draft.falsification_criteria: Falsified if, holding the used framework inputs (lsd_f, lsd_p, AV) fixed, adsorption entropy loss does not increase with the anisotropy descriptor over its training range, or if the apparent anisotropy effect disappears once Vol (overall size) is controlled for, indicating size rather than shape drives the loss. Also falsified if elongated guests in straight-channel frameworks retain rotational entropy (free rotation about the long axis after alignment), giving the opposite sign in that regime. Boundary check: single-site guests (PMI1 = PMI3 = 0) must show the minimum descriptor value 0; if these guests show nonzero relative rotational loss attributable to shape, the proxy mapping fails.

review_issues.explanation: Dimensional inconsistency in the formula: the regularization adds a dimensionless constant 1.0 to PMI3 + PMI1, which carries native units of amu*angstrom^2. The rationale claims the descriptor is a 'dimensionless ratio of native quantities', but with the +1.0 term it is not strictly dimensionless unless 1.0 is implicitly read as 1 amu*angstrom^2. This is the stated basis of the execution_check rejection ('incompatible dimensions in addition, subtraction, minimum or maximum'). The implicit unit assignment and the magnitude of the regularization constant are unstated empirical choices, recorded here without correction.

Zero-count alignment is unresolved: training statistics show PMI1 zero_n = 113 and near_zero_n = 268, while rotor_proxy_counts give single_site = 54 and linear = 214. The boundary narrative assumes single-site guests are the all-zero case and linear guests have PMI1 = 0, but the mapping between the reported zero counts and rotor classification is not established by the provided data. The descriptor's behavior at the boundary depends on this unresolved mapping.

Unverified proxy-to-mechanism mapping: the hypothesis maps heavy-atom implicit-H principal-moment anisotropy to 'orientation-dependent rotational hindrance'. This mapping is not demonstrated by any cited source; the inputs are proxies, not measurements of lost rotational freedom. Additionally, the descriptor does not distinguish prolate (rod-like) and other elongated geometries with the same (PMI3 - PMI1)/(PMI3 + PMI1) value but potentially different rotational hindrance, so the claimed mechanism does not uniquely follow from the descriptor value. The draft acknowledges the competing free-rotation-about-long-axis expectation; the mechanism remains unvalidated for this dataset.

Rotor-case structure not separated: the single descriptor mixes single-site (zero rotational entropy in the gas phase by construction), linear (two rotational degrees of freedom), and nonlinear rotors without an explicit rotor_case branch. Linear guests with PMI1 = 0 receive near-maximal anisotropy (descriptor approximately PMI3/(PMI3+1), approaching 1 for typical PMI3 magnitudes), which reflects a gas-phase rotational degree-of-freedom difference as much as a confinement effect; the descriptor cannot separate these contributions. Formula rules require explicit rotor_case for native single-site/linear/nonlinear inertia use; the draft applies a single regularization constant across all cases.

E02 support is indirect: the mechanism card cavity_rotation (E02) lists proxy_inputs lsd_f, lsd_p, GeDi and reports cavity-diameter comparisons (FER ~4.3 A vs FAU ~13 A); it contains no connection to principal-moment anisotropy. There is no knowledge-graph edge from cavity_rotation to PMI1/PMI3, so the cited E02 support for a PMI-based shape descriptor is an extrapolation from cavity size to adsorbate shape. Per review scope this absent edge is recorded as unknown support, not as disproof.

E06 support is an extrapolation: the source proposes comparing the radius of gyration of each molecule against available cavity space in MCM-22 supercages, for linear and singly branched adsorbates, with diffusion discussion at 450-850 K. It does not propose a principal-moment anisotropy ratio, and its conditions (MCM-22 supercage regime, molecule subset, temperature range) are not this dataset's regime. Transfer of the proposed rotational-freedom comparison to an anisotropy descriptor across all frameworks is unproven.

E03 supports only that both translational and rotational motions contribute to adsorption entropy losses; it provides no direction, sign, or shape dependence for the anisotropy effect. Citing E03 supports the mechanism family (rotation as a contributor) but not the specific monotonic prediction of the descriptor.

Confound between shape and size is acknowledged but unresolved within the descriptor: the falsification criteria require controlling for Vol to distinguish shape from size effects, but Vol is not part of the formula and no such control is implemented in the descriptor itself. The physical_prediction holds lsd_f, lsd_p, and AV fixed, but these inputs are not used in the formula, so the 'at fixed framework geometry' conditioning is an interpretive claim about the analysis rather than a property of the expression; the conditional direction (increasing loss with PMI3 at fixed PMI1) is arithmetically monotonic for the expression alone.

Boundary behavior is finite and mostly as stated, but interpretation at the boundary is definition-dependent: at PMI1 = PMI3 = 0 the descriptor maps to 0, which the draft interprets as 'rotationally spherical / no rotational entropy to lose' for monatomic guests; this interpretation is consistent for single-site guests only if the all-zero samples are indeed single-site (see unresolved zero-count issue above). For linear guests with PMI1 = 0 the descriptor tends toward its maximum rather than an intermediate value, which the boundary narrative's phrase 'descriptor in (0,1)' does not quantify; with training-scale PMI3 values (median ~125), the value is approximately 0.99, effectively saturating. Recorded as an interpretive limitation, not corrected.

The execution_check status is 'rejected' on dimensional grounds while scientific_consistency is 'unverified' and mechanism_validated is false. Whether the rejected status reflects the +1.0 dimensional issue alone or additional checks is not resolvable from the provided data. This review records the inconsistency without adjudicating the rejection or modifying the draft.

draft.name: pmi_anisotropy_reg
draft.hypothesis: Conditional hypothesis (rotation/shape family): at fixed framework geometry (e.g., fixed lsd_f, lsd_p, AV), adsorbates with larger principal-moment anisotropy (PMI3 - PMI1)/(PMI3 + PMI1) lose a larger fraction of their gas-phase rotational entropy upon adsorption, because anisotropic (elongated or disk-like) guests have orientation-dependent accessibility: rotations about the short axes sweep a volume comparable to the molecular length/width scale and are more strongly hindered in pores than the nearly isotropic rotations of compact guests. This generalizes the reported MFI-vs-FAU rotational-loss comparison (E01, E04) and the FER/FAU cavity-confinement comparison (E02), and follows the MCM-22 proposal to compare molecular rotational freedom via a molecular size/shape measure (radius of gyration) against the available cavity space (E06), consistent with rotation being a distinct contributor to entropy loss alongside translation (E03). This is an empirical, unverified mechanism for this dataset, not an established law; the competing expectation that a rod aligned in a straight channel rotates freely about its long axis is explicitly acknowledged as a falsification route.
draft.rationale: PMI3 and PMI1 are heavy-atom, implicit-H inertia proxies, not full all-atom moments; the +1.0 (in the native amu*angstrom^2 scale) is a fixed regularization constant that keeps the descriptor finite at legitimate physical zeros (single-site atoms with all PMIs = 0 map to 0, i.e., rotationally spherical, which is physically appropriate since a monatomic guest has no rotational entropy to lose). Because it is a dimensionless ratio of native quantities, no q-normalization is needed and no q-ratio is misread as a physical equality threshold. The descriptor is a shape proxy only; it does not encode pore size, so any claimed effect is conditional on holding the framework inputs fixed. It does not duplicate the round-2 size-vs-bottleneck descriptor (q_Vol**(1/3)/q_lsd_f) and targets a different mechanism family (rotation rather than translational size confinement).
draft.falsification_criteria: Falsified if, holding the used framework inputs (lsd_f, lsd_p, AV) fixed, adsorption entropy loss does not increase with the anisotropy descriptor over its training range, or if the apparent anisotropy effect disappears once Vol (overall size) is controlled for, indicating size rather than shape drives the loss. Also falsified if elongated guests in straight-channel frameworks retain rotational entropy (free rotation about the long axis after alignment), giving the opposite sign in that regime. Boundary check: single-site guests (PMI1 = PMI3 = 0) must show the minimum descriptor value 0; if these guests show nonzero relative rotational loss attributable to shape, the proxy mapping fails.

draft_candidate.name: pmi_anisotropy_reg
draft_candidate.hypothesis: Conditional hypothesis (rotation/shape family): at fixed framework geometry (e.g., fixed lsd_f, lsd_p, AV), adsorbates with larger principal-moment anisotropy (PMI3 - PMI1)/(PMI3 + PMI1) lose a larger fraction of their gas-phase rotational entropy upon adsorption, because anisotropic (elongated or disk-like) guests have orientation-dependent accessibility: rotations about the short axes sweep a volume comparable to the molecular length/width scale and are more strongly hindered in pores than the nearly isotropic rotations of compact guests. This generalizes the reported MFI-vs-FAU rotational-loss comparison (E01, E04) and the FER/FAU cavity-confinement comparison (E02), and follows the MCM-22 proposal to compare molecular rotational freedom via a molecular size/shape measure (radius of gyration) against the available cavity space (E06), consistent with rotation being a distinct contributor to entropy loss alongside translation (E03). This is an empirical, unverified mechanism for this dataset, not an established law; the competing expectation that a rod aligned in a straight channel rotates freely about its long axis is explicitly acknowledged as a falsification route.
draft_candidate.rationale: PMI3 and PMI1 are heavy-atom, implicit-H inertia proxies, not full all-atom moments; the +1.0 (in the native amu*angstrom^2 scale) is a fixed regularization constant that keeps the descriptor finite at legitimate physical zeros (single-site atoms with all PMIs = 0 map to 0, i.e., rotationally spherical, which is physically appropriate since a monatomic guest has no rotational entropy to lose). Because it is a dimensionless ratio of native quantities, no q-normalization is needed and no q-ratio is misread as a physical equality threshold. The descriptor is a shape proxy only; it does not encode pore size, so any claimed effect is conditional on holding the framework inputs fixed. It does not duplicate the round-2 size-vs-bottleneck descriptor (q_Vol**(1/3)/q_lsd_f) and targets a different mechanism family (rotation rather than translational size confinement).
draft_candidate.falsification_criteria: Falsified if, holding the used framework inputs (lsd_f, lsd_p, AV) fixed, adsorption entropy loss does not increase with the anisotropy descriptor over its training range, or if the apparent anisotropy effect disappears once Vol (overall size) is controlled for, indicating size rather than shape drives the loss. Also falsified if elongated guests in straight-channel frameworks retain rotational entropy (free rotation about the long axis after alignment), giving the opposite sign in that regime. Boundary check: single-site guests (PMI1 = PMI3 = 0) must show the minimum descriptor value 0; if these guests show nonzero relative rotational loss attributable to shape, the proxy mapping fails.

draft_candidate.proxy_assumptions: Assumes heavy-atom implicit-H principal moments rank the true rotational freedom of the full molecule well enough for a monotonic proxy; assumes the anisotropy ratio (not absolute moment magnitude) captures orientation-dependent hindrance independent of guest size; assumes framework confinement strength is captured by the held-fixed inputs lsd_f/lsd_p/AV and that Df (passing bottleneck) and Dif (included along free path) are distinct from a global cavity diameter, so no cavity-Di equality is claimed. These are proxy assumptions under the conditional mechanism cards, not established causality.
draft_candidate.boundary_behavior: Finite on the full training support: denominator PMI3 + PMI1 + 1.0 >= 1.0 for all native inputs, so no division by zero at the 54 single-site zero-PMI samples (descriptor = 0 there) or for linear guests (PMI1 = 0, descriptor in (0,1)). Legitimate physical zeros are preserved, not imputed; the regularization constant is a fixed numerical choice, stated as empirical.

appended.name: size_bottleneck_confinement_ratio
appended.hypothesis: At fixed framework bottleneck (lsd_f), a larger adsorbate (larger Vol, hence larger Vol^(1/3)) is more geometrically confined at the framework bottleneck, so a larger fraction of its gas-phase translational/rotational entropy is lost on adsorption, increasing loss = (Sgas - Sads)/R. Equivalently, at fixed adsorbate volume, frameworks with a larger passing free-sphere bottleneck (lsd_f) impose weaker confinement and smaller entropy loss. This is a conditional geometric-confinement hypothesis motivated by reported FER/FAU and MFI/FAU comparisons (E02, E04), not an established law for this dataset.
appended.rationale: Vol^(1/3) converts the van der Waals volume into an isotropic linear size proxy; lsd_f (Zeo++ Df) is the largest sphere that can pass through a periodic free path, i.e., the tightest geometric constraint on guest passage, not the global cavity diameter Di. The ratio proxies the tightness of geometric confinement without claiming a literal free-volume equality: both factors are length-like, the ratio is dimensionless, and both native inputs are strictly positive over the entire training support (Vol in [20.424, 161.144] angstrom^3; lsd_f in [0.85684, 7.68726] angstrom), so no native-zero handling is required. Known limitations: (i) Df is a bottleneck, so a molecule can sit in a large cage behind a narrow window and this descriptor then overestimates local confinement; (ii) Vol^(1/3) ignores molecular anisotropy, which PBF/PMI/SPAN would capture but only with rotor_case branching and legitimate zeros; (iii) AV is deliberately not used because it is mass-specific fixed-probe accessibility, not molecule-specific free volume.
appended.falsification_criteria: The hypothesis is falsified if, holding Vol fixed, the learned loss decreases with this descriptor (opposite sign to confinement), or if the association vanishes once probe-accessible area/volume (q_ASA, q_AV) are controlled for, indicating the descriptor only re-expresses accessibility rather than bottleneck confinement. A competing explanation to rule out: descriptor behavior driven entirely by lsd_f correlating with framework density rather than any adsorbate-size dependence (check by testing whether the Vol dependence holds at fixed lsd_f).
appended.proxy_assumptions: Assumes (1) geometric confinement at the tightest passage is a relevant driver of adsorption entropy loss, by analogy to reported cavity-diameter/rotational-entropy-loss comparisons, which used cavity diameters, not Df — this proxy mapping is assumed, not demonstrated; (2) Vol^(1/3) is an adequate isotropic molecular size proxy; (3) q-normalization with fixed positive training references preserves monotonic ordering (q_Vol and q_lsd_f are strictly positive scalings). No causal claim: the descriptor is an empirical proxy and the direction of the target association is a hypothesis to be tested.
appended.boundary_behavior: Finite training support: q_Vol in [(20.424/67.24), (161.144/67.24)] and q_lsd_f in [(0.85684/5.16326), (7.68726/5.16326)], both strictly positive, so the ratio is finite and strictly positive everywhere in the training domain. No native zeros occur for either input, so no legitimate-zero preservation issue arises; the descriptor is undefined only outside the physical domain (Vol <= 0 or lsd_f <= 0), which does not occur.
